---
title: "Architecture overview"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
This project draws smooth decorative curves — scrolls, leaves, ribbons — and it
does so with two tools rather than one. They are good at different things, and
most of the design decisions follow from keeping them apart.

## The curve engine (`curve_lab`)

A train does not jerk into a bend; the track eases into it. That transition is a
Euler curve, or Euler spiral, and the engine uses the same idea for ornament.

The engine's job is the *drawn* curve: it fits smooth Euler-curve segments, gives
them width, and checks that separate strokes do not collide. Its joins are G1 by
construction — the tangents meet exactly. Curvature is continuous (G2) only
where a terminal's width law or a blend supplies it; a plain corner or a
junction without a blend still has a curvature step, and the reports say so.

You use it through the web interface (`web/`), which edits a design, previews
it, reports on it, and downloads SVG.

## The spine layer (`pythagorean-spiral`)

Computers count in decimals, and a few hundred accumulated rotations leave a
closed loop a fraction off its start. The spine layer avoids that by choosing
its rotations from whole-number right triangles. A 3-4-5 triangle turns by an
angle whose sine and cosine are exactly 3/5 and 4/5, so rotating a point is
`(4x - 3y, 3x + 4y) / 5` — no trigonometry, no rounding. Every heading and
every node is rational, and a chain closes on an exact grid line.

What that buys, and what it costs:

- The **plan** is exact: the turn schedule, the closure, the apsis, the joints
  and the mirror are integer or rational facts.
- The **drawing** can be exact too, but only for chains small enough to afford
  the arithmetic. Past a few hundred chords the coordinates are computed in
  doubles, with a measured residual around 1e-13 — far below the page.
- A right angle is exact as a *cusp*, a component swap; it is not reachable by
  accumulated turning, which is a theorem, not a limitation of the code.

The spine layer is not an Euler curve and does not replace the engine. It is a
polygon whose headings match an Euler curve at the nodes; its position is up to a
chord away.

## How they are meant to connect

The intended pipeline, from exact plan to finished page:

```text
1. SKELETON        pythagorean-spiral
   exact spine from whole-number turns
   closure and endpoints on the grid
            |
            v  anchors and headings
2. INK             curve_lab
   smooth segments, width, rails, clearance
            |
            v  paths
3. PREVIEW         web/
   edit, measure, download SVG
```

**All four conditions hold under the author's fidelity rule (2026-10-30).** The two tools now
meet at `curve_lab/spine.py`: a chain's own spans become ordinary Euler curve
segments, so rails, terminals, clearance and the SVG writer need no second
geometry kind.

1. **Done.** `curve_lab` imports a chain and builds a `Piece`/`Trace` from its
   anchors; every fitted join lands on a chain anchor (worst 2e-14 units).
2. **Done.** `workbench/spine-sheet.html` draws a curl on the 200 × 250 mm sheet
   through `svg.document`.
3. **Done.** `piece_clearance()` measures the same build; a contact declared at
   a forked node passes, and the same gap fails without the declaration.
4. **Done.** One W03 study is drawn entirely from Pythagorean chains. P01's
   start heading (77.97°) and corners are not in any triangle's rotation group,
   so this is a chain plan, not P01's node table. It passes the author's
   rule — worst span-end drift at most **1.6% of study height** — at **1.29%**
   with a 0.5° turn step. See `FIDELITY.md`; the study is **not** node parity
   (0.03 units for the port against 19.44 here).

There are now **two profiles** of a chain study: the exact one (one cubic per
chord, 1,164 cubics) for zooming and choosing, and the practical one (one
Euler curve per structural run, 34 cubics at 0.42 mm) for output. A **pin** carries
a branch chosen on the exact curve into the practical curve as an exact vertex.
The remaining gap is surface, not wiring: the fill currently needs the spine
layer's exact miter, because the engine's rail builder crosses at per-chord
corners.

## Two systems, three ways in

The tool has two curve systems and three ways to enter them. The distinction
matters, because only two of the three are different geometry.

| way in | you supply | it solves | it produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| **spine** | a triangle, a turn schedule, a closure | an exact rational Euler polygon | a chain → `Piece` |
| **engine** | segments, points with tangents, or recovered spans | the Euler curve through those constraints | a `Design` → `Piece` |
| **scroll** | an end radius, a join gap, a page and a clearance | the curvature rate and the length, plus the inflection or the return to radius `r` | a `Design` → `Piece` |

The spine is a *different* curve: a discrete polygon with exact rational nodes.
The engine and the scroll share one equation, `kappa(s) = kappa0 + kd*s`; the
scroll is a front end that turns a designer's numbers (circle radius, gap, page)
into that equation, instead of asking for `kappa0`, `kd` and a length or for a
list of points. It is the volute/scroll family, not a fourth kind of ink.

The practical consequence: a scroll should emit an ordinary `Design`, so it
inherits the rails, terminals, clearance, SVG writer and the practical curve's
pins. Today it lives in `scripts/spiral_turns.py`; the next step is to promote it
to `curve_lab/scroll.py` with tests, and then it is a first-class way in
rather than a page experiment.

## Where to look

| If you want | Read |
|---|---|
| Why the project exists and in what order | [The plan](/docs/project/) |
| To use the browser tool | [Web application guide](/docs/web-guide/) |
| A plain-English term | [Glossary](/docs/glossary/) |
| The words, and how the two sides' vocabularies map | [Glossary](/docs/glossary/) |
| What is true today, and what is next | Current truth (`state/HANDOFF-int.md`) |
| The spine layer, step by step | [Spine guide](/docs/spine/) |
| The curve model in detail | [Curve model](/docs/curve-model/) |
| The accepted accuracy budget | [Fidelity](/docs/fidelity/) |
| The recovered plates and their formats | [Recovered corpus](/docs/corpus/) |
| Work items, plates and decisions | Work items and the work board (`state/WORK-int.md`) |
| What passes, and how | [Verification](/docs/verify/) |
| What works today | Status (`state/STATUS-int.md`) |
| Who wrote the engine | [Credits](/docs/credits/) |
| The spine layer in depth | Spine explainer (`pythagorean-spiral/docs/EXPLAINER.md`) |
| How the folder is organised | [Documentation index](/docs/index/) |

## Which tool for which job

| You want to | Use | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Sketch a curve and see it | web app | `web/`, and the app's own page |
| Download an SVG for Inkscape | web app | the download control |
| Close a loop that must meet exactly | spine layer | Spine explainer (`pythagorean-spiral/docs/EXPLAINER.md`) |
| Snap a flourish to an exact grid | spine layer | Spine explainer (`pythagorean-spiral/docs/EXPLAINER.md`) |
| Look up a term | — | [Glossary](/docs/glossary/) |

## What this overview does not claim

- That the engine is G2 everywhere. It is not; see above.
- That a chain study is P01. It passes the 1.6% fidelity rule and is not node
  parity; see `FIDELITY.md`.
- That "exact" means the coordinates at any scale. It means the plan; the ink is
  measured.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/glossary.md -->

---
title: "Glossary"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
The two sides of the project use different words for overlapping ideas. This
page defines each word as the code uses it, then maps the two vocabularies. It
is the only vocabulary list the repo keeps: the shorter one it used to defer to
was never written.

## The curve engine (`curve_lab`)

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **Piece** | One drawing: named traces, an optional mirror, layers, and declared contacts. It is the container, not a claim that the ornament is finished. |
| **Trace** | One full line inside a piece: a spine, its optional ribbon width, its terminals, and its mirror rule. |
| **Segment** | One piece of a design's centre line: an Euler curve arc stated by `kappa0`, `kd` and `length`. |
| **Contact** | A *declared* legal touch or crossing. The clearance report allows a crossing only where a contact covers it. |
| **Section** | A reading, not a shape: one station across a full line, with the spine point, tangent, width and the two rails. |
| **Bundle** | The design box: a named set of full lines that must not touch, with an internal clearance and a footprint. The box is for placement, not clipping. |
| **Terminal** | The umbrella for how a line ends: caps (which close without turning past 120°) and tapers. |

## The spine layer (`pythagorean-spiral`)

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **Anchor** | One node's exact point and exact heading. Every node has one, not only the start. |
| **Node framework** | That anchor plus its tangent and normal: the datum a branch, cap or terminal attaches to. A view of the anchor, not a second store. |
| **Spine** | The drawn curve through the anchors: equal chords, each turned by a whole number of triangle angles. Not "skeleton". |
| **Knot** | A span boundary where two cubics meet. It is a location, not a guarantee that the join is smooth. |
| **Rail** | An offset edge giving the spine width. In the spine layer it is a miter offset of exact points; rational for small chains. |
| **Cusp** | A quarter turn made by swapping coordinates, `(x, y) -> (-y, x)`: exact, and the only way to get a true right angle. |

## How the vocabularies line up

| Purpose | Engine | Spine layer | Plain English |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where a line starts and which way it points | design `anchor` | anchor | the same idea; the spine's is always rational |
| The path before width | the trace's spine | spine | the backbone line |
| Where two pieces meet | segment join | knot (span boundary); node framework at a branch | a location, with an attachment datum on the spine side |
| The width's edges | offset rails | miter rails | lines pushed outward to make a ribbon |
| A finished drawing | `Piece` | a placed spine with rails | the spine has no `Piece` equivalent yet |
| A group that must not touch | `Bundle` | no equivalent yet | a design box on the engine side |

Two mismatches are worth stating rather than papering over: the spine layer has
no finished-drawing container, and no bundle. Both are promotion-gate work.

## G0, G1 and G2

| Grade | Meaning | Where it is true here |
|---|---|---|
| **G0** | The ends touch; directions differ. A corner or a spike. | a cusp, or a declared corner |
| **G1** | Directions match; curvature steps. | the engine's joins, by construction |
| **G2** | Directions and curvature match. | where a width law or a blend supplies it; not at every corner |

The spine layer adds a different kind of guarantee: at a shared node the two
sides read the *same stored point and heading*, so the join is exact before any
curve is drawn. The drawn cubics are still an interpolation, within about 1.4%
of the ideal curvature law.

## Words to avoid

- **Skeleton** — say spine.
- **Hermite** — say interpolated spine, except in one parenthesis.
- **Frame** for the attachment datum — say node framework. "Frame" still means
  the render frame (`--frame WxH`) or coordinate axes.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/curve-model.md -->

---
title: "The curve model"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
The engine draws one line at a time. You give it a starting point, a direction,
and a list of segments; each segment bends by a stated amount, and that bend
changes steadily along its length. It then wraps that line in a complete drawing
so it can have thickness, shaped ends, a mirror image, and a list of places where
it is permitted to touch another line.

## The recipe: a `Design`

At the data level a curve is a JSON object with an anchor and an ordered list of
segments:

```json
{
  "anchor": {"x": 40.0, "y": 80.0, "angle": 0.0},
  "segments": [{"length": 40.0, "kd": 0.002, "kappa0": 0.0}]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `anchor` | Where the line starts on the sheet (`x`, `y`), and which way it points (`angle`). |
| `segments` | The pieces of the line, in drawing order. |
| `length` | How long this segment is along the curve, in millimetres. |
| `kd` | How quickly the bend changes along the segment (`dκ/ds`). Positive turns left, negative turns right, zero is straight. |
| `kappa0` | How tightly the line is bending at the start of this segment. |

> **What curvature means.** It is a number for how tight the bend is: small is
> nearly straight, large is a tight curl. Setting `"kappa0": null` means "carry
> on with the bend the previous piece ended with", so the line does not jolt at
> the join.

Coordinates and units:

- distances in **millimetres**;
- angles in **radians**;
- angle `0.0` points **east**;
- **+y increases upward** from the bottom of the sheet.

## The drawing: a `Piece`

- **`Piece`:** the top-level drawing. It holds named traces, an optional global
  mirror (overridable per trace), layers, and a list of declared contacts.
- **`Trace`:** one full line: its centreline path, its ribbon width, the shapes
  at its two ends, and whether it is mirrored.

`render_piece()` builds every trace once and writes one SVG, so the sheet (the
standard 200 × 250 mm page), the scale and the upward +y orientation are decided
in a single place.

## The ends: terminals

**Terminal** is the general word for how a stroke finishes.

- **Caps** close a line without turning it more than 120°: `butt` (cut square),
  `point` (sharpened), `arc` (a 5 mm dome), `round` (a half-width dome).
- **Tapers** narrow the line over a set distance: `taper` (linear), `cone`
  (pointed), and `bulb` (the legacy Stage II width profile, not an ornamental
  wrapped bulb).
- **Turned terminals** curl back further than 120° — a volute eye, a scroll, a
  coiled end. *Planned; not built.*

## Corners, joins and junctions

- **Fillet:** rounds an angular corner with a short circular arc that touches
  both edges. The line and the arc meet in the same direction (G1), but the bend
  changes abruptly where the arc starts and where it ends.
- **Junction:** a branch meeting a trunk at a declared merge. A junction carries
  the corner, the gap that must survive inside the fork, the rounding or blend,
  the taper, and the contacts where the strokes are allowed to touch.
- **Euler curve blend:** the easing transition that would remove the sudden change
  in bend at a junction. *Planned; not built.*

## Measuring across the line: `Section` and `Bundle`

- **`Section`:** one slice across a line at a point along its length: the
  centreline point, the direction, the width, and the left and right edges.
- **`Bundle`:** a group of named lines that must keep a stated minimum gap and
  not touch. It has a footprint for placing the group as one unit; the footprint
  does not clip anything.

## Gaps and collisions: clearance

Clearance measures the closest distance between two strokes and lists
everywhere they cross.

- **Intended touches.** Two lines may touch or cross only where a `Contact` is
  declared. A contact has a point, a radius, the two line names, and it waives
  the clearance rule *inside* its radius only; outside, the rule applies.
- **Unintended collisions.** A crossing with no contact is reported as an
  interference.
- **Tolerances.** Every measurement carries a small margin, so the report says
  **pass**, **warning** or **violation** instead of pretending to know the last
  hundredth of a millimetre.

## How lines meet

| Grade | Name | In plain words |
|---|---|---|
| **G0** | positional | The ends touch, but the lines point in different directions: a corner or kink. |
| **G1** | tangent | They point in the same direction, so there is no corner, but the tightness of the bend changes suddenly. |
| **G2** | curvature | They point the same way *and* bend by the same amount: an invisible transition. |

**What the engine actually does.** By construction, every join in
`curve_lab` is **G1**. True **G2** appears only where a width law or a
deliberate blend provides it; an unblended corner or junction still has a
curvature step, and the reports say so.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/ph-integer.md -->

---
title: "Integer PH curves: the generator, the grid, and what is actually true"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
A corrected version of a survey that has been circulating in this project.
Where it agrees with the arithmetic it is kept; where it does not, the number
below was computed, not remembered. Every figure on this page comes from
`scripts/generators.py`, which works in `fractions.Fraction` and asserts that each
coordinate is integral before it writes anything.

## The generator

A planar curve has a *Pythagorean hodograph* when the speed is a polynomial:

```
x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2 = sigma(t)^2
```

Every such curve is written, with complex polynomials `w = u + iv` and a factor
`h`,

```
z'(t) = h(t) · ( u(t)^2 - v(t)^2 ,  2 u(t) v(t) )
sigma = h(t) · ( u(t)^2 + v(t)^2 )
```

and Farouki and Sakkalis's lemma fixes the degree:

```
n = deg h + 2 · max(deg u, deg v) + 1
```

That identity is the load-bearing one, and the survey omitted it — which is why
its quartics and sextics had no construction. With `h = 1` only odd degrees
appear; the `h` factor is the only way to reach an even degree:

**The three names, once.** **PH** is a planar curve whose speed is a polynomial.
**PHH** is the PH quintic Hermite interpolant through two points with prescribed
endpoint tangents. **PPH** is piecewise PH: PH spans joined with C² continuity.
All three are 2D here, and their definitions, the full ladder, the integer hits
and the interpolant/spline constructions live in one place:
`workbench/ph-families.html`, built by `scripts/ph_families.py`; the geometry is
`curve_lab/ph_hermite.py`. This page keeps the arithmetic that page quotes.

| `deg h` | `max(deg u, deg v)` | degree |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 3 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 |
| 0 | 2 | 5 |
| 2 | 1 | 5 |
| 1 | 2 | 6 |
| 0 | 3 | 7 |
| 1 | 3 | 8 |

## What comes free

With integer generators, and no approximation anywhere:

- **speed** is the polynomial `h (u² + v²)`;
- **arc length** integrates it exactly, as a polynomial;
- **tangent** is `2·atan(v/u)`, or in integers, Euclid's doubling
  `(u²−v², 2uv) / (u²+v²)`;
- **offset** by a distance `d` is *rational*, not refitted;
- **curvature** is a rational function;
- **splitting** at any `t` keeps the curve PH and keeps the generators integral.

## The integer arithmetic

Control points come from integrating the hodograph, so the cubic divides by 3,
the quartic by 4, the quintic by 5, the sextic by 6 — then a conversion to the
Bernstein basis multiplies by binomials. Milestones at `t = k/m` bring the
Bernstein weights, which carry `m` to the degree. The least integer that clears
both is the scale.

What that means in practice, for four curves built from small numbers:

| curve | n | generators | step | scale | integer grid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cubic | 3 | `h=(1)` `u=(2,-2)` `v=(1,-2)` | 1/4 | 24 | 32 × 32 |
| quartic | 4 | `h=(1,2)` `u=(1,-1)` `v=(1,-2)` | 1/4 | 1536 | 1152 × 1280 |
| quintic | 5 | `h=(1)` `u=(-2,-1,1)` `v=(-1,-1,2)` | 1/2 | 480 | 1872 × 1744 |
| sextic | 6 | `h=(1,2)` `u=(-1,1,0)` `v=(2,-1,0)` | 1/2 | 240 | 880 × 640 |

Three consequences, and they contradict the folklore.

**The milestone scale is `mⁿ`, and PH never improves it.** A plain Bézier whose
control points are integers already has integer control points at scale 1, and
pays exactly the same `mⁿ` for its milestones. PH *costs* a factor of 3
(cubic) or 15 (quintic) on the control points, because the integration
denominator has to be cleared. What PH buys is exact arc length, rational
offsets and a rational frame — not a smaller lattice.

**Integer milestones always exist.** Any finite set of rational parameters
clears at the lowest common multiple of its denominators. The bean, for
example, has quarter-points with denominators 1, 91, 3, 91 and 1, so a scale of
273 puts every one on the grid. The scale is a fact about the arithmetic, not a
wall.

**What is impossible is the strong claim.** No bounded curve holds infinitely
many lattice points, so "infinitely many points on the curve can be integers"
cannot be true of any curve, PH or not. You get finitely many, at parameters
you choose.

## The numbers that circulate

| claim | what it is | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| cubic, fifths, scale 750 | 375 for `u=(2,1)`, `v=(1,2)` | 2× too high |
| quintic, fifths, 3,125 | `5⁵`, the step term | a floor, not the scale |
| quintic, fifths, 187,500 | `2²·3·5⁶`, one generator set | true of some numbers only |
| quintic, tenths, 3,000,000 | `10⁵ = 100,000` is the step floor | 30× too high |
| "2, 4, 8, 16 at eighths → 128" | a cubic at eighths is at least `3·512` | not reproduced |
| arc length 26 for the worked example | 26 is the unscaled sum; ×3 gives 78 | off by the scale |

None of these are fatal — they are all the same error, which is treating a
number that belongs to *one set of generators* as if it belonged to the degree.

## Degree by degree

- **n = 2** does not exist. There are no quadratic PH curves.
- **n = 3** is the Tschirnhausen cubic, up to scale and rotation: one shape
  only, no inflection, so a C-curve. Loops and cusps are reachable by letting
  the generators cross.
- **n = 4** needs `deg h = 1`. It can inflect, which the cubic cannot.
- **n = 5** is the workhorse: C and S shapes, first-order Hermite interpolation
  with a single segment, and the only low degree that supports C² PH splines.
  The quintic transition curve — straight line to circular arc with monotone
  curvature — is the lowest-degree polynomial that does the Euler curve's job.
- **n = 6** takes `deg h = 1` with quadratic generators. This is where the
  multiple-cusp shapes live.

## Named curves

Two of these are nodal cubics, and only one is the PH one. Every cubic PH curve
is a scaled, rotated *Tschirnhausen cubic*, `27ay² = (a−x)(8a+x)²`, whose node
crosses at 60 degrees. The other, `y² = x²(x+1)`, crosses at 90 — same genus,
same degree, reachable from the first only by an affine map, never by a
similarity, because an angle is not affine. A cubic PH curve's control polygon
is what the top of this page has been building; the node angle is how you tell
whether a nodal cubic is that family or merely nearby.

The test that separates these is rationality, and it is decidable: count the
singular points, and check that the gradient vanishes at each. A rational curve
has an exact Bézier — substitute `t = s/(1−s)` and clear denominators. A curve
with a cusp does not, and sampling is the honest fallback.

| curve | equation | degree | tier | integer data |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bean | `x⁴ + x²y² + y⁴ = x(x² + y²)` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 12, milestones 273 |
| bicorn | `y²(1 − x²) = (x² + 2y − 1)²` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 6, milestones 105 |
| pear | `x² = y³(1 − y)` | 8 | rational · exact Bézier | control 35, milestones 625 |
| heart | `(x² + y² − 1)³ = x²y³` | 6 | not rational · sampled | — |
| nodal | `y² = x²(x + 1)` | 3 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 1 |
| tschirnhausen | `27y² = (1 − x)(8 + x)²` | 3 | rational · exact Bézier | control 1, milestones 27 |
| bow | `x⁴ = x²y − y³` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 16 |
| epicycloid k=3 | `x = 4cos θ − cos 4θ,  y = 4sin θ − sin 4θ` | 8 | rational · exact Bézier | control 35, milestones 1 |
| epicycloid k=5 | `x = 6cos θ − cos 6θ,  y = 6sin θ − sin 6θ` | 12 | rational · exact Bézier | control 231, milestones 1 |
| deltoid | `x = 2cos θ + cos 2θ,  y = 2sin θ − sin 2θ` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 1 |
| hypocycloid k=5 | `x = 4cos θ + cos 4θ,  y = 4sin θ − sin 4θ` | 8 | rational · exact Bézier | control 35, milestones 1 |
| nephroid | `z ↦ z³ + 3z on the unit circle` | 6 | rational · exact Bézier | control 5, milestones 1 |
| astroid | `(x² + y² − 1)³ + 27x²y² = 0` | 6 | rational · exact Bézier | control 5, milestones 1 |
| trifolium | `(x² + y²)² − x³ + 3xy² = 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 12, milestones 50 |
| quadrifolium | `(x² + y²)³ = (x² − y²)²` | 6 | rational · exact Bézier | control 15, milestones 125 |
| circle | `x² + y² = 1` | 2 | rational · exact Bézier | control 1, milestones 5 |
| rounded square | `four edges and four quarter arcs` | 4 + 4 pieces | rational · exact Bézier | control 1, milestones 425 |
| squircle | `|x|⁴ + |y|⁴ = 1` | 4 | not rational · sampled | — |
| cardioid | `(x² + y²)² + 2x(x² + y²) − y² = 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 25 |
| bernoulli | `(x² + y²)² = x² − y²` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 4, milestones 41 |
| gerono | `x⁴ − x² + y² = 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 6, milestones 25 |
| cruciform | `x²y² − b²x² − a²y² = 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 1250, milestones 1081080 |
| piriform | `x⁴ − 2x³ + y² = 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 25 |
| abs(x) gerono | `x⁴ − x² + y² = 0, x ≥ 0` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 25 |
| piriform 2x | `x⁴ − 2x³ + y² = 0, x → 2x` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 25 |
| semicubical | `y² = x³` | 3 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 27 |
| cissoid | `y²(2 − x) = x³` | 3 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 16575 |
| kappa | `(x² + y²)y² = x²` | 4 | rational · exact Bézier | control 1, milestones 6718930400 |
| strophoid | `y²(1 + x) = x²(1 − x)` | 3 | rational · exact Bézier | control 3, milestones 195 |

The bean is worth spelling out. In polar form it is `r = cosθ / (1 − ¼sin²2θ)`,
a ratio of polynomials; with `t = tan(θ/2)` and `t = s/(1−s)` it becomes an
exact rational Bézier whose homogeneous control values are whole numbers, and
it reproduces the curve to `10⁻¹⁶`. Its two `W = 0` control values are points at
infinity, which is why there is no control *polygon* to lay on the lattice.

The piriform is the fourth exact one. Its equation is `a⁴y² = b²x³(2a − x)`,
which at `a = b = 1` is `y² = x³(2 − x)`: a rational quartic with a cusp at the
origin, a vertex at `(2, 0)`, and the bounds `0 ≤ x ≤ 2`, `|y| ≤ 3√3/4`.
Through `x = 1 + sin t`, `y = cos t (1 + sin t)`, then `u = tan(t/2)`, the
homogeneous generator is `X = (u+1)²(1+u²)`, `Y = (u+1)²(1−u²)`, `W = (1+u²)²`
— whole numbers, no clearing needed.

Two wrong forms are worth recording, because both look plausible. The quartic
`x⁴ − x²y + y² = 0` is a quadratic in `y` with discriminant `−3x⁴`, so its only
real point is the origin; and `x⁴ + x²y − y² = 0` factorises as
`(y − k₁x²)(y − k₂x²)` with `k = (1 ± √5)/2` — two parabolas, not a pear. Only
the `x³` form is the curve.

## The catenary

A true catenary is `a·cosh(x/a)`: transcendental, so no scale factor can put it
on an integer grid, and the AHPH family keeps the PH property in a hyperbolic
basis — exact arc length, rational offsets — but not integers.

**This is solved, on its own page.** `workbench/catenary.html` builds the
catenary two ways and neither pretends to be a single integer curve:

- **four PH cubics** over the curve, exact at both endpoints and both tangents,
  worst error **0.41 per cent of `a`**;
- an **integer chord walk** where the heading snaps to a rung of the 3-4-5
  ladder and each chord is the hypotenuse of a real triangle, so every node is a
  whole number on the lattice.

That is the answer, and it is recorded in `state/ACHIEVEMENTS-int.md`. Do not solve
it again.

## What this session measured

Two results, both negative, both worth keeping.

**The discriminant route does not produce a lattice.** It is true that a
segment's closure quadratic has a rational square discriminant exactly when the
fit is exact. But on the full 92-rung pythagorean ladder, for the four catenary
chords, **0 of 17,168** non-negative discriminants are squares; and where one
is, `k` carries a denominator in the thousands, so the control points are
rational, not integral. Choosing the pair buys exactness, not integers.

**The generator route does.** You do not fit through prescribed points and hope;
you choose integers and the endpoint is whatever it is. That is the difference
between `scripts/generators.py` and a least-squares fit.

Along the way `from_pairs` in `scripts/hodograph.py` turned out to rotate by
half the tangent angle, so it only closed when a segment started at zero. It is
fixed and now agrees with `from_hermite` to `10⁻¹⁴`.

## Open

- Whether the named curves should be fitted to a measured reference with a
  stated tolerance, in the manner of `FIDELITY.md`.
- Whether the named curves should be fitted to a measured reference with a
  stated tolerance, in the manner of `FIDELITY.md`.
- Whether `generators` should write straight into the web app's input pages.

---
title: "Verification"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
Four checks. Each answers one practical question, and each can fail on its own.

## 1. Does the curve engine still work?

```sh
.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover tests
```

239 tests: curve geometry, pieces, ends, junctions, clearance, the web API, the
shared-token gate, and the work board's principle cards. When they pass, the
engine still does what it says.

Read the last line of the output for the current count. A number pasted into a
document goes stale; the command is the source.

## 2. Does the spine layer still work?

```sh
cd pythagorean-spiral && ../.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
```

139 tests: exact closure, the exponent dial, joins and forks, the rails, large
drawings in ordinary decimals, placement, and a frozen digest of the legacy curl
so its shape cannot drift by accident.

*Status:* last run 2026-10-29, all passing.

## 3. Do the local and deployed copies match?

```sh
.venv/bin/python scripts/check-parity.py
```

Compares the served files, presets, caps, the drawing and the report between the
local server and the deployed copy. Both must be running. This is a standalone
audit and is never run during a handoff.

## 4. Do the pages fit small screens?

```sh
node scripts/check-web.mjs
```

Draws the documentation pages and the app at 900, 390 and 320 pixels wide, and
fails if anything overflows sideways. It starts its own headless Chrome; single
screenshots use `scripts/shot.mjs`, which launches its own browser through
Playwright — nothing needs to be running first.

## What passing does not mean

Passing shows the code follows its rules without crashing or breaking an
invariant. It says nothing about how the result looks:

- how naturally a curve sweeps along its chords;
- how closely a transferred cap matches its source plate;
- how a veil or a fill reads to the eye.

Those are recorded as measured studies in the documentation. Read the numbers
there; they are evidence, not tests.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/fidelity.md -->

---
title: "Fidelity: the accepted budget"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
> **Important — author decision, 2026-10-30.** A chain that imitates a
> An Euler curve is accepted at **1.4–1.6 per cent**. That figure was set for the
> curvature-law fit (the chain follows the ideal Euler law to 0.8% of peak; the
> drawn cubics to 1.4%, rms 0.8%). For a **chain study** the working rule is:
> the worst span-end drift must be **at most 1.6 per cent of the study's
> height**. State the metric whenever the number is quoted. It is a budget for a
> resemblance, **not** node parity with the source drawing.

This page exists because the same question — “is this close enough?” — has now
been answered once, and the answer was nearly lost. Future work should reuse the
rule instead of re-litigating it.

## The number that was already accepted

From the spine layer's own handover:

> Measured on the curl's entry run: the chain follows κ = κ₀ + kd·s to **0.8 %
> of peak**; the drawn cubics to **1.4 % (rms 0.8 %)**. It is an Euler spiral to
> a percent and a half.

That is the precedent: about one and a half per cent, for a chain standing in
for an Euler curve. It was accepted as good enough for ornament at print size.

## Two different percentages, and why the difference matters

The original **1.4%** is a *curvature-law* figure: how far the drawn curve's
bending departs from the ideal Euler spiral over a run.

The **chain-study rule** measures something else: the distance between each
span end and the source drawing's node, as a percentage of the study's height.

They have the same magnitude and the same purpose — “close enough to read as the
same ornament” — but they are not interchangeable. A future report must say
which one it is using. Do not compare a node drift against the 1.4% curvature
figure as if they were the same measurement.

## What a chain study must report

Every chain study page and test must carry:

- the turn step (the triangle's angle),
- the chord count,
- the drift at every span end, not only the worst,
- the worst drift in units **and** as a percentage of the study's height,
- how long the build took, so the cost is visible,
- a plain statement of what the study is **not** (P01 parity, in the first case).

## The measurement (study 01, right half)

Measured in P01's own frame, start heading snapped to the nearest whole turn.
The reference is the ported P01; the study height is 1510 units.

| turn step | chords | worst drift | of height | build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2° | 62 | 66.19 units | 4.38% | 0.08 s |
| 1° | 115 | 21.38 units | 1.42% | 0.08 s |
| 0.5° | 221 | 19.44 units | **1.29%** | 0.25 s |
| 0.25° | 431 | 20.76 units | 1.38% | 1.45 s |
| 0.125° | 852 | 1.67 units | **0.11%** | 9.44 s |
| 0.0625° | — | did not finish in 60 s | — | — |

The coarse steps are **not** monotone, and that is not a wall: the errors from
independently rounded corners can add or cancel, so 0.5° happens to beat 0.25°.
At 0.125° the grid is fine enough that the residual collapses to 0.11%. The
limit is cost, not principle: the exact fraction arithmetic grows with the chord
count, and 0.0625° did not finish in a minute.

So the honest statement is: **finer triangles do converge, and cost rises
steeply.** An earlier note in this repository said the drift “does not fall with
the angle”; that was wrong and has been corrected. It was based on runs that
stopped at 0.25° and on a 0.1° run that timed out.

## The rule

1. Choose the turn step and report it.
2. Build the study.
3. Measure every span end against the source.
4. **Pass** if the worst drift is at most **1.6% of the study height**; report
   the number either way.
5. If it fails, the honest options are: a finer step (with its cost), shorter
   chords, or the float hybrid. Never smooth the difference away silently.

Under this rule study 01 at 0.5° passes at **1.29%**. The same study at 0.125°
passes with a wide margin at **0.11%**, at 852 chords and about nine seconds for
the composite alone.

## What this rule does not license

- It does **not** make the chain study P01. The ported P01 matches its reference
  to **0.03 units**; the chain candidate is **19.44 units** at 0.5° — about 650
  times further. Calling the candidate “P01” would be false.
- It does **not** make the chain exact ink. The plan is rational; the chord
  lengths for arcs are rational approximations of `2R sin(α/2)`, and the page is
  floats.
- It does **not** settle the fill. A ribbon width on a per-chord chain crosses at
  the corners under the engine's rail builder; the filled shape is the spine
  layer's miter job (`ribbon.outline`).

## Two profiles, one shape

The exact profile is the chain itself: one straight design segment per chord,
and therefore one cubic per chord. At a 0.5 degree step that is 943 design
segments and **1,164 cubics** with the mirror, a 249 KB page. It is the file to
zoom into and to keep as the record.

The practical profile fits one Euler curve through each *structural run* — the part
between two of the study's corners — and subdivides a run only when the measured
error exceeds the tolerance. At 0.5 mm:

| profile | design segments | cubics with mirror | page | worst deviation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| exact | 943 | 1,164 | 249 KB | reference |
| practical, no pin | 18 | 34 | 7 KB | 0.42 mm |
| practical, one pin | 19 | 36 | 7 KB | 0.32 mm |
| practical at 0.25 mm | 22 | 42 | 8 KB | 0.23 mm |
| practical at 1.0 mm | 16 | 30 | 6 KB | 0.92 mm |

`curve_lab/practical.py` builds it; `workbench/practical-curve.html` compares it
with the exact curve.

## Pins: choosing a branch on the exact curve

The exact curve is where you zoom in to choose a branch point. The practical
curve cannot be a fixed simplification, because a branch must land on a real
vertex with the exact heading.

A **pin** is that choice: a point on the exact chain (or its knot index) made a
hard split in the practical fit. Both sides of the pin use the chain's outgoing
heading; the rest of the curve is re-simplified within the same tolerance. The
measured pin error is about **2e-7 units**, and the tangent is continuous across
it, so the branch joins without a correction. Adding one pin costs one or two
cubics.

Workflow: choose on the exact curve → pin the point → regenerate the practical
curve → attach the branch.

## How that compares with type

A capital C in a serif face is **not** two or three cubics; that is a geometric
ring, not a letter. Measured native counts from ten installed serif faces:

| face | C | @ | & | ~ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Times New Roman | 21 | 55 | 45 | 14 |
| Baskerville | 19 | 46 | 42 | 12 |
| Didot | 38 | 82 | 70 | 24 |
| Bodoni 72 | 34 | 51 | 47 | 10 |
| Big Caslon | 42 | 68 | 94 | 12 |
| Charter | 18 | 56 | 32 | 16 |
| Hoefler Text | 23 | 49 | 48 | 14 |
| Iowan Old Style | 20 | 56 | 48 | 16 |
| New York | 28 | 71 | 47 | 18 |
| PT Serif | 32 | 69 | 64 | 16 |

TrueType stores quadratics, and one cubic reproduces a quadratic exactly by
degree elevation, so the count is the cubic equivalent. One serif C is 18–42
cubics; `@` is 46–82 and `&` is 32–94. The practical half at 14 Euler curves is in the
range of one serif C; the exact half at 221 is past a whole glyph, and the band
at 722 is past an `@` several times over.

## The fitter bug behind the old count

The first exact measurement was inflated by a real bug: at a segment boundary
the backend reports the *next* segment's tangent, so a corner corrupted the end
of the previous cubic and the fitter kept splitting to hide it. Reading the
tangent just inside the segment fixed it. One straight segment now takes one
cubic, not nine.

## Where the rule came from

The author set it on 2026-10-30, in the same conversation that produced the
promotion gate. Record it here, in `state/SESSIONS-int.md`, and in the public docs; it is
the kind of decision that is expensive to rediscover.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/clearance.md -->

---
title: "Clearance and crossings"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
`curve_lab/clearance.py` answers one question about a drawing:

> Does the ink keep at least **5 mm** between strokes, and does it cross
> anywhere it was not allowed to?

It is a measurement, not a constraint solver. Nothing moves to satisfy it; the
report tells you where the drawing fails and by how much.

## Vocabulary

| Word | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| **clearance** | the minimum edge-to-edge distance the design must keep |
| **spacing** | centreline distance; `clearance + (w₁ + w₂)/2` for two ribbons |
| **counter** | the white shape the clearance creates (the bulb beside a terminal) |
| **contact** | a declared place where two strokes may touch or cross |
| **instance** | one trace, or the mirror of one; ink that belongs together |
| **ink** | rails and terminal caps. Spines are construction lines and are excluded by default |

## Quick start

```python
from curve_lab.clearance import Contact, piece_clearance

result = piece_clearance(piece, clearance=5.0, tol=0.05)

if not result["ok"]:
    for bad in result["violations"]:
        print(f"{bad['a']} / {bad['b']}: {bad['distance']:.2f} mm "
              f"({bad['shortfall']:.2f} mm short) at {bad['at']}")
```

Allowing a legal junction where a leaf meets a branch:

```python
result = piece_clearance(
    piece, clearance=5.0,
    contacts=[Contact((12.0, 0.0), radius=2.5,
                      a="ink/leaf", b="ink/branch")],
)
```

`result` is a plain dict: `ok`, `min`, `violations`, `warnings`, `crossings`,
`disallowed`, `clearance`, `tolerance`, `margin`, plus `piece` and `fit_ok` when
called through `piece_clearance()`.

## How the decision is made

Flattening introduces a known error: a polyline is within `tol` of its curve, so
the measured minimum can be up to `2·tol` below the true one. The report keeps
that honest instead of rounding it away:

| Measured distance | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `< clearance − 2·tol` | **violation** — definitely too close |
| `clearance − 2·tol … clearance + 2·tol` | **warning** — inside the uncertainty band |
| `> clearance + 2·tol` | pass |

At `clearance = 5`, `tol = 0.05`: violation below 4.9, warning from 4.9 to 5.1.
The warning band is not noise — it is the only responsible answer when the
measurement cannot resolve the last tenth of a millimetre.

## Junctions waive clearance inside their footprint

A junction is not a violation; it is a merge. A `Contact` therefore carries
`waives_clearance=True` by default: a pair closer than the rule is accepted when
**both strokes pass within the contact's radius**, and the pair is listed under
`merged` rather than dropped. Testing the footprint rather than one sampled
closest point matters: the minimum between two parallel rails is a whole line,
and the first point found is arbitrary. The gore — the narrowing gap just outside
the footprint — is still measured normally, which is the point: the waiver has
an edge, and the edge is where the drawing must start respecting the rule again.

Pass `waives_clearance=False` for a contact that only permits a crossing while
still demanding the gap.

## Why instances matter

A 6 mm ribbon has two rails 6 mm apart and a cap that meets both at the tips.
Measuring those as separate strokes would call every piece a violation. Groups
are therefore compared only **between** instances (`Group.instance`), never
within one. The mirror is its own instance, so the gap between a trace and its
reflection is measured, which is what a fleur half demands.

`piece_clearance(..., roles=("rail", "cap"))` is the default. Spines are
excluded because they are construction geometry and usually closer together
than the ink; pass `roles=("spine", "rail", "cap")` to include them.

## API

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `piece_clearance(piece, ...)` | build the piece once, measure the ink, return the report |
| `measure(groups, ...)` | the same judgement on groups you built yourself |
| `Contact(point, radius, a=None, b=None)` | declare a legal touch, optionally for one pair of instances |
| `flatten(spans, tol)` | polyline for a span chain, within `tol` |
| `segment_distance(p1, q1, p2, q2)` | closest points of two segments (Ericson §5.1.9) |

## Algorithm

1. **Build once.** `build_piece()` returns `Group` objects — spine, rail or cap,
   tagged with their instance — and `render_piece()` writes SVG from the same
   list. Measurement and drawing cannot drift apart.
2. **Flatten.** Each cubic is split by de Casteljau until its control points are
   within `tol` of the chord (or a depth cap of 18 is hit). The bound is
   conservative; it never reports a polyline further from the curve than `tol`.
3. **Compare instances.** For each pair, minimum segment-to-segment distance.
   The bounding boxes are used only to skip the crossing scan when the boxes are
   disjoint; the distance is always computed so `min` is the true minimum.
4. **Find crossings.** Segment intersections, including collinear overlap.
   Touching endpoints count as crossings: that is how an undeclared contact
   looks. Each is allowed only if a `Contact` covers it.
5. **Classify.** Violations, warnings, allowed and disallowed crossings.

Complexity is `O(n·m)` in flattened segments per instance pair. A piece with a
few hundred spans measures in milliseconds; a whole catalogue would want an
AABB index, and the engine already has one internally.

## Limits and non-goals

- **No self-intersection test within an instance.** A ribbon's own rails are
  checked elsewhere: `build_rail()` reports `folds` and a `margin`, and a
  terminal refuses a folded ribbon.
- **No curvature or tangent check.** Gaps are distance only. Smoothness is the
  job of `engine`'s join report.
- **Contacts are declared, never inferred.** A drawing that happens to touch is
  a violation until someone says it is a junction.
- **Clearance is per pair of instances.** Three-way crowding is reported as the
  three pairwise minima, which is sufficient for the rule.
- **Polyline geometry only.** Curvature extrema between sample points can hide a
  sub-tolerance dip; choose `tol` below the smallest feature you care about.

## Tests

`tests/test_clearance.py` — 26 cases: segment distances (parallel, crossing,
collinear, endpoint, degenerate), flattening bound, pass/warn/fail bands, the
same-instance exclusion, mirror gap, disallowed crossing, declared contact,
named contacts, argument validation, report shape, clearance waivers inside and outside a contact.

## Where this goes next

A junction object (leaf → branch → trunk) will declare its contacts through
this module, and the gore is read directly from the warning band: the set of
points where two strokes come within `clearance` of each other.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/junction.md -->

---
title: "Junctions"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
A junction is where one stroke meets another: leaf to branch, branch to trunk.
The vocabulary is borrowed, because the problem is older than this project:

| Word | Source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **fillet** | engineering | the blend arc at a corner |
| **crotch** | botany | the white wedge where a branch leaves a stem |
| **gore** | road design | the triangular white between diverging carriageways |
| **haunch** | architecture | the thickening where a member meets its support |
| **bulb** | this project | a width law at a terminal, swelling into the gap |
| **cap** | drafting / SVG | a *subset* of terminal: closes the end without turning the stroke past the cap limit |
| **turned terminal** | this project | a terminal that turns past the limit (hairpin, wrapped bulb) — not a cap |

The cap limit is currently **120°**, chosen for this project and free to move;
it is a threshold, not a theorem. Under it: `butt`, `point`, `arc` and `round`
are caps; `taper`, `cone` and `bulb` are tapers; a hairpin is a turned terminal.

## What exists now

`curve_lab/fillet.py` — the circular fillet, and nothing more.

```python
from curve_lab.fillet import corner_fillet

f = corner_fillet(a=(10, 0), corner=(0, 0), c=(0, 10), radius=2.0)
f["start"], f["end"]     # (2, 0), (0, 2) — the touch points
f["centre"]              # (2, 2)
f["trim"]                # how much of each edge the arc consumes
f["spans"]               # cubic spans, start → end
```

`fillet_span(spans, index, radius)` does the same in place: it trims two
straight spans at their shared corner and inserts the arc, so the result is one
continuous chain.

`arc_segment(f)` turns the fillet into a circular-arc `Segment` and anchor, so
it can enter a `Design` chain and be rendered by the same writer as everything
else:

```python
from curve_lab.fillet import arc_segment
from curve_lab.model import Design, Segment

spec = arc_segment(f)
design = Design(anchor=..., segments=[Segment(kd=0, length=8, kappa0=0),
                                      Segment(**spec["segment"]),
                                      Segment(kd=0, length=8, kappa0=0)])
```

The two joins come out G1 with a curvature step of `1/r` — exactly what a
circular fillet is, and the reason a trunk eventually wants the Euler curve
blend.

The maths is the standard construction: for interior angle `θ`, the touch
distance is `T = r / tan(θ/2)`, the centre sits on the bisector at
`r / sin(θ/2)`, and the arc turns through `π − θ`. It refuses a radius that does
not fit the shorter edge, collinear edges, and edges that double back.

## What it is not

- **It is G1, not G2.** Curvature jumps from 0 to `1/r` at each touch point.
  That is honest for a foot or a nick, and visible on a trunk. The Euler curve
  blend (`cl_g2_connect` in the engine) is the next step, not this one.
- **Straight edges only.** `fillet_span` rejects curved spans instead of
  pretending a tangent point lies on the chord.
- **No clearance check.** A fillet can still crowd a neighbouring stroke. Run
  `piece_clearance()` on the result; the fillet does not police itself. At the
  junction itself, declare a `Contact` with `waives_clearance=True` so the merge
  is accepted and reported under `merged`, while the gore outside the footprint
  is still measured.

## The junction object

`curve_lab/junction.py` now has it:

```python
from curve_lab.junction import Junction

j = Junction(corner=(0, 0), branch_end=(30, 0), trunk_end=(0, 40), radius=6)
built = j.build()          # {"piece", "contact", "report"}
report = built["report"]   # angle, tangent, arc length, trim, join "G1", 1/r
result = j.check()         # the clearance report, merge declared
```

The branch is a straight run, the fillet arc, and the merge; the trunk is a
straight ribbon. The contact at the merge carries `waives_clearance=True`, so
the overlap is accepted and reported under `merged` — while anything crowding
the junction from outside still fails. The reported join is **G1**: that is the
circular fillet, stated rather than dressed up.

## What comes after this object

```text
Junction
  point        where the two centre lines would meet
  angle        interior angle between the strokes
  clearance    minimum gap that must survive through the crotch
  fillet       radius, or None for an Euler curve blend
  taper        length over which the branch narrows into the trunk
  bulb         none | cone | bulb, from the W02 terminal laws
  contacts     declared Contact objects passed to the clearance report
```

Its report should carry the join grades (G0/G1/G2), the minimum clearance
through the gore, the bulb's maximum width, and any crossing not covered by a
declared contact. That is the point where "leaf joins branch" stops being a
drawing and becomes something the tests can hold.

## Beta-splines as a join option (not built)

A **Beta-spline** is the geometric-continuity alternative to solving a join.
Instead of forcing the curvature to match, the join carries two shape
parameters — conventionally β₁ (a tangential scale) and β₂ (a tension, or
curvature ratio) — and the pieces are constructed so the join is G2 for any
positive values of them. B-splines are the special case β₁ = 1, β₂ = 0.

Why it matters here: the current G2 route is the fillet or the Euler curve blend,
both of which *solve* for the matching curvature. A beta-spline instead exposes
the joint as two dials, which is closer to how a capital or a leaf-to-branch
join is actually adjusted. The cost is the same as every spline: the result is
a piecewise polynomial, not an exact named curve, so it cannot join `NAMED` and
must be declared.

It is recorded here, not implemented. If it is adopted it belongs beside
`corner_fillet`, as a `join=` option with β₁, β₂ and the resulting G2 report —
not as a curve family. Source: Barsky, *Computer graphics and geometric
modeling using Beta-splines* (1988); the shape-parameter formulation is also in
the geometric-continuity literature (e.g. the ACM survey on geometric
continuity, shape parameters and constructions).

## Prior art, without copying

- `focus-math/repos/kurbo/kurbo/src/stroke.rs` — how joins are built in general.
- `focus-math/repos/spiro/` — G2 interpolating spirals; the global alternative.
- `focus-math/notes/05-junctions-and-fillets.md` — the full reading list.
- SolveSpace / FreeCAD sketchers (GPL/LGPL) — reference for arc-tangent
  constructions only.

## Tests

`tests/test_fillet.py` — 19 cases: right angle and 60°, arc on the circle,
continuity, clearance from the corner, radius fit, collinear and doubled-back
rejection, trimming two spans, keeping the outer ends, curved-span rejection, arc-segment endpoints and curvature, and the G1 join
report.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/philosophy.md -->

---
title: "Design philosophy"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
The question this answers: when we say "a fleur", what is the object, in what
order is it built, and what are its parts called?

## The logic of beauty

Beauty is not an optional accessory.

Take a simple black square on a white background, say a piece of paper. Stare at
the square for a little, then look at the white part of the paper. You see a
floating square. If you just look at the square continuously, you notice the
edges seem to have the same effect as when you looked at the white part of the
paper: a halo effect. This is because of the way our eye is constructed; the
receptors get tired, and so a shadow shape is formed.

When we add a beautiful frame to the square, we are softening the effect of
tiredness in our eyes. The halo effect is swallowed up by the ornate part of the
frame. Frames are often gold coloured not to show richness, but because the halo
often has a golden or reddish-brown luminance.

The same with a diploma on the wall, with an engraved outside edge — it makes it
easier to look at.

The line weight has to vary, and different colours help as well. This keeps the
halo effect to a minimum.

When we look at a window, we get the same effect in reverse: the light from the
window creates a halo or shadow effect when we look away. Stained glass windows
soften that effect, when they are done right.

Another thing beauty does is orient us. Usually they help us retain balance by
literally showing us which way is up. Often beautiful designs are symmetric
side to side but they are different on top than they are on the bottom.

The consequences for this project: **the frame is not decoration around the
curve, it is the part that lets the eye rest.** A uniform hairline is the case
the eye tires of first, which is why the plates want two weights and a mid tone,
and why a border that collides with its centre reads as a fault however correct
the geometry.

## The glyph is a graph, not a walk

There is no single curve to walk from 1 to 2 to 3. A glyph is:

    glyph   = parts + joints + symmetry + measurement
    part    = a full line (stroke body) with two terminals
    joint   = a declared contact between two parts
    symmetry= mirror, applied to the whole glyph
    measure = clearance, crossings, folds

Order of drawing is **layer order**, not connectivity. Order of building is
**part by part**, each part walked once along its spine. A fleur is not "trace
the outline"; it is "a lance, two petals, a band, a foot, two tails, mirrored,
with declared joints between them".

## The full line

The three lines together — centre and both rails — are a **full line**.

- **spine** — the centre line, the curve the engine computes.
- **rail** — either edge. `rail +` is on the left of travel, `rail −` on the
  right, with left = `(-t.y, t.x)` for tangent `t` (y up).
- **full line** — spine + both rails + the width law that relates them. This is
  the unit of design, measurement and naming ("the petal's full line").
- **stroke** is reserved for what SVG means: the drawn mark. Using it for the
  body would collide with `stroke-width` and `stroke-linecap` in every file.

**Direction is part of a full line.** A stroke is walked from its *start*
terminal to its *end* terminal, and the rails are named by that direction.
Mirroring reverses handedness: the mirror's left rail is the original's right.
A terminal is therefore never just "the end"; it is the start or the end.

## Sections, not independent walks

At one station `s` along the spine, the three lines are one cross-section:

    section(s) = (left, spine, right, tangent, curvature, width)

This is the "design box" idea, and it is how the model should *think*: width,
terminal width laws, clearance and folds are all properties of a section or a
pair of sections. The rails are **derived at the same stations**, never walked
separately and never independently re-timed.

Rendering is allowed to disagree in representation, not in meaning: each rail is
fitted to cubics for SVG, so the output is three paths that no longer share a
parameter. That is fine — the authoring model is section-locked, the output is
path-locked. Measurements take the fitted paths and carry their error bound.

## Infinity, linearity, curve

Every design carries three aspects. They may live in different parts, but all
three must be present:

- **linearity** — a section with zero curvature: a straight run, a line, a
  chord. It is the rest in the phrase.
- **curve** — a section whose curvature *changes*: an Euler span, a LAC, a
  petal. An arc is bent, but a circle has constant curvature, so it is one
  limit case, not the whole of the aspect.
- **infinity** — a tendency the stroke approaches and does not reach: a spiral
  whose curvature tends to a circle's, a heading that tends to a limit, a line
  whose direction is a point at infinity. Infinity is a tendency, not a
  vanishing point and not a decorative taper.

A design with only two is incomplete: a circle alone is all curve, a cross
alone is all line, a plain spiral is curve plus infinity with no rest. The rule
is about the whole design, not every part: a straight stem can supply
linearity, a petal the curve, and a spiral tail the infinity.

Examples:

| object | linearity | curve | infinity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Euler curve / Euler | κ → 0 at one end | κ grows | the heading limit |
| LAC | the low-curvature start | the power-law bend | the limiting circle |
| 3-4-5 exact chain | straight chords | triangular-number headings | the open spiral's limit |
| integer cubic | straight end tangents | the S bend | **absent** — pair it with a spiral or a ray |
| fleur | band and lance | petals | **absent** — needs a spiral tail or ray |
| volute proof | the straight chords | the growing headings | the open spiral's limit heading |
| cruciform proof | the arms | the fillets | **absent** — needs a ray or a spiral tail |
| ending-fit sheet | the stalk | the sections | n/a — a measurement, not a design |
| modulated-width sheet | the spine | the width law | n/a — a measurement, not a design |

The last two rows are recorded gaps, not rejections: the cubic and the fleur
are legal parts, and a design that contains one must supply the missing aspect
elsewhere. Name the three aspects on the page or in the notes. A missing aspect is a gap
to fill, not a silent pass. The rule applies to **designs**; a measurement or
catalogue page states the aspects of the objects it measures, but is not
itself a design.

## Grounded

Every design must be grounded: it has a horizontal datum — a ground line,
baseline, plinth, band or foot — and a vertical element (stem, lance, axis,
trunk) whose relation to that datum is stated. The relation may be visible
(drawn) or invisible (declared in the construction), but it may not be absent.

- **visible:** the fleur's band and foot; the cruciform's horizontal arms; a
  plant stalk's ground line.
- **invisible:** the volute's start tangent as the ground and its 90° heading
  as the vertical; the integer cubic's horizontal chord and its vertical arm
  tangents.

A design that floats — a curve with no ground and no vertical — is incomplete.
Name both on the page or in the notes: "ground: …; vertical: …".

| design | ground | vertical |
|---|---|---|
| fleur | band + foot | lance |
| cruciform | horizontal arms | trunk |
| volute | start tangent (declared) | 90° heading (declared) |
| integer cubic | chord P0–P3 | arm tangents |
| plant stalk | baseline / grid | stalk |
| modulated width | endpoint horizontals | spine |

## Lattice: points and stations

Two different things are called "a lattice hit". Keep them apart:

- a **lattice point** — both coordinates are integers. This is the strong
  claim, and it is what cuts, joins, branches and exact nodes need.
- a **lattice station** — one coordinate is an integer: the stalk crosses a
  horizontal grid line. This is what a growth mark needs, because the mark sits
  at a place on the stalk, not at a point that must be integer in both axes.

Measured on the plant-form stalk (the proof's unit-scale curve, y from 0 to 8):
**seven** horizontal crossings at y = 1…7, and **none** of them has an integer
x; the only full lattice point on the whole stalk is its start (0, 0). On the
3-4-5 lobe, 2 of 11 nodes are integer at scale 1, and all 11 are integer at
×9,765,625. A rule that demanded full points for marks would put one mark on
the proof stalk and none on most real stems.

So: marks at **stations**, exact operations at **points**. Never call a
station a lattice point in a page or a note.

## Terminals

- A **terminal** is any treatment of a full line's end.
- A **cap** is the subset that closes the cross-section without turning past the
  cap limit (120° for now, tunable).
- A **taper** closes by narrowing: `taper`, `cone`, `bulb` (the width-law bulb).
- A **turned terminal** goes past the limit: hairpin, wrapped bulb. Not caps.

Terminals belong to ends, not to traces: `(start, end)` is part of the model.

## Joints

A **joint** is where two full lines meet: leaf into branch, branch into trunk.
It is declared, never inferred from proximity. Declaring it does two things:

1. it permits the crossing or merge inside its footprint;
2. it waives clearance *inside* that footprint, and only there.

The **gore** is the part of the gap just outside the footprint; it is measured
normally, which is what keeps a junction from hiding crowding. The **counter**
is the white shape the gap makes — the bulb beside a terminal is a counter.

## Mirror

The mirror is a symmetry of the glyph, not a second drawing. It duplicates
every part whose rule says it is mirrored, and swaps the handedness of terminals
and rails. The centre seam is a joint like any other: if the two halves touch,
that contact is declared.

## What this rules out

- **No global walk.** No 1,2,3 around the outline; no imposed starting point.
- **No implicit joins.** Two strokes that happen to touch are a violation until
  declared.
- **No rail-first design.** A rail is always a section of a full line, never an
  independent curve that the spine is inferred from.
- **No style in geometry.** Width is geometry (a law), not a stroke attribute.

## Where the code stands

| Idea | In code |
|---|---|
| glyph = parts + joints + mirror | `Piece` (traces, contacts, mirror) |
| full line | `Trace` + width; rails built as `Group`s |
| section | `section.py`: `Section`, sampled by arc length |
| terminal (cap / taper / turned) | `terminals.py`; turned not built |
| joint | `Contact`, `Junction` |
| measurement | `clearance.py` |
| grammar | `grammar.py` (study 01) |

The read model is `Section`; the grouping object is `Bundle`. It is what a terminal width law, a
junction gore and a clearance sample all want to read, and today each of them
reconstructs it from the fitted paths.


<!-- source: app/src/content/docs/docs/primal.md -->

---
title: "Primal ornaments"
---

> **draft A** — a working draft, not a final text.
A category of its own, after the framework and before the archetypes:

    framework → primal (fire, water, earth, air) → archetypal (fleur, acanthus)

**Primal** means elemental: one force, one grammar. **Archetypal** means
cultural: a fleur-de-lis, an acanthus leaf, a palmette — forms that carry
history and composition, not a single physical idea.

The primal set is where the framework is proved against nature rather than
against an existing drawing. Four elements, four studies, one parameter family
each.

## The gate: what "framework is done" means

No primal work starts until all of these are true:

1. **W03 complete** — the twenty fleur studies render from parameter sets, with
   node parity against the old generator.
2. **Terminals complete** — caps, tapers *and* turned terminals (hairpin,
   wrapped bulb), with the cap limit enforced.
3. **Joints** — a junction with a declared contact, a measured gore, and the
   clearance report passing outside the footprint.
4. **Sections** — `Section` exists as a first-class read model, so width laws
   and clearance sample the same stations instead of reconstructing them.
5. **Reachable** — a primal study can be authored, measured and rendered
   through the web app, not only from a script.

Until then this page is intent, not a plan of record.

**Status 2026-10-26:** the first slice exists ahead of the gate, by request —
`curve_lab/primal.py` and `workbench/primal.html`: one canonical grammar per
element (earth terraces with corners, a water wave, cloud billows, a fire
tongue), rendered from Euler-curve segments with the terminals each needs. They
are sketches to argue with, not the studies described above: no parameter
families, no measured gores, no web route. The gate still stands for those.

## The four, and what each one tests

| Element | Grammar | What it forces the framework to prove |
|---|---|---|
| **Earth** | strata, roots, facets: long straight runs, true corners, thick-to-thin bands, taper to a point | corner handling (`Segment.corner`), taper laws, heavy/light balance |
| **Water** | flow, parallel waves, droplets: long low-curvature sweeps, bulbs, reflections | section-locked parallels, bulb law, round and teardrop terminals |
| **Air** (cloud) | billows and curls: big arcs into spirals, scalloped edges, light tapers | spiral chains, round caps, clearance between adjacent billows |
| **Fire** | licking tongues: high curvature, hairpins, sharp points, asymmetry | turned terminals, the 120° cap limit, folds at tight radii |

Order of work: **earth → water → air → fire**. Earth is cheapest and tests what
is already built; fire is last because it needs the turned terminals, and it is
the one that will expose any weakness left in the other three.

## What "one study" means

Each element gets the same shape of deliverable as a fleur study:

- one canonical drawing (the acceptance test),
- three to five parameter sets that read as one hand,
- the terminals it needs, named from the existing vocabulary,
- its joints declared, with the gore measured,
- a page under `docs/` with the drawing, the measurements and the parameters.

No fills. Ink on paper, y up, millimetres, one sheet.

## Relationship to the archetypes

The primal studies are not ornaments to copy; they are grammars to reuse. A
fleur's petals are closer to water than to fire; an acanthus is closer to earth
and water than to air. When the archetypes start, their spans should come from
the primal vocabulary — scroll from air, leaf from water, foot and band from
earth — rather than from new special cases.

## Where this sits in the work board

The work board's work items stop at W26. When the gate above is met, this becomes
**W27 — primal studies** (with W28+ for the four elements if they need separate
tracking), and the archetype work follows as W29. Do not add plates to the work board
before their grammar exists; that is the mistake the catalogue already shows.


<!-- source: state/DESIGN-int.md -->

# DESIGN-int — decisions already taken, and why

Read before changing a control, a page or an ordering. Each line is a decision,
the reason it was made, and its status. **Settled** means do not re-open it
without the operator saying so in words. **Open** means it is a live question.

Dates are the day the decision was made. Where the operator asked for it, the
entry says so.

## Speed numbers (the boxes and their sliders)

- **Two sliders per speed number: mantissa and decade.** Settled 2026-11-14, by
  the operator. The mantissa slider (red) sets the size 0–10, the decade slider
  (blue, 64 px) sets the power of ten −2…6. Reason: large numbers are quick to
  reach; the mantissa alone cannot get to 1000 or 0.01 without the buttons.
  Twenty-four sliders at degree 11 is correct, not a bug.
- **The sign lives in the number box, not the slider.** The slider carries size
  only; the `−` button flips the sign. Reason: a slider through zero would make
  zero sit in the middle, which reads as "set to middle" when the value is
  nothing.
- **Scale buttons stay beside the sliders** (`√2`, `×1.1`, `e`, `×1`, `×10`,
  `×100`). Reason: the decade slider is coarse; these are the exact snaps.
- **The power labels follow the step, written as fractions.** At step ½ the six
  boxes read `t^0`, `t^1/2`, `t`, `t^3/2`, `t^2`, `t^5/2`; at step ⅓ they read
  `t^0`, `t^1/3`, `t^2/3`, `t`, `t^4/3`, `t^5/3`. The worked formula under the
  page and the closing line use the same names. Reason: a box labelled `t^2`
  that carries `t^1` is a lie. Fractions, not decimals, so `t^5/2` never becomes
  the rounded `t^2.5`. Settled 2026-11-14.
- **The exponent step is a slider with named buttons** on the experimental page
  only: 1, ½, ⅓, ¼, plus any value between (0.75 gives `t^0.75`, `t^1.5`,
  `t^2.25`). Settled 2026-11-14.

## The roots panel and the ruler

- **A flat spot is a root.** The wording on the page and in this repo: a root of
  the y speed is where the stroke runs horizontal. Settled.
- **Mirror is on by default.** One click at `1/9` places `1/9` and `8/9`.
  Reason: symmetry has to be put in on purpose; a random row almost never has
  it. Settled.
- **Dots stack for multiplicity.** Three dots at `1/2` is the triple flat, which
  is what makes the long flat middle. Settled.
- **Click the line to add; click a dot to remove that copy; shift-click clears
  the stack.** Settled 2026-11-14, by the operator ("click on the dot again and
  it disappears"). Dots sit clear of the line so the line stays clickable.
- **`fill the numbers` multiplies the roots out** and picks the rung that fits
  (five spots → degree 11, six → degree 13). Reason: the row is the polynomial
  the spots multiply to; nobody should type it by hand.
- **A fractional bow scales both rows** by its denominator, and the status line
  says so. Reason: a common scale leaves the shape alone and keeps every number
  whole.
- **Ruler positions are fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10
  and 12**, mirrored about `1/2`. Settled.
- **Sliders for `copies at 1/2` (0–6) and `bow` (−4…4)** sit under the ruler.
  Settled 2026-11-14.

## Pages

- **`ph-nth-sandbox.html`** — part 1: the degree ladder, a gallery of the seeds
  and whatever the finder wrote.
- **`ph-nth-sandbox-2.html`** — part 2: the **Knotlike curves** section first,
  then everything else.
- **`ph-nth-sandbox-exp.html`** — experimental, **no gallery at all**, exponent
  step defaults to ½. Reason: a curve under test must not sit among the ones we
  keep. Settled 2026-11-14, by the operator.
- **The knotlike section leads with the operator's six pasted curves**
  (`wave3`, `knot`, `bud`, `knot-2`, `wave5`, `hersheys copy`), tagged *yours*,
  then the finds tagged *found*. Reason: the finds are compared against them,
  not instead of them. Settled 2026-11-14.
- **Order inside the finds: most meetings with the partner copy first, then the
  cheapest grid, then the lowest bend.** Reason: meetings is the knot measure;
  among equals the cheap grid is the better curve. Settled 2026-11-14.
- **Moves are stored by name in the generator**, never by hand-editing the page:
  `DEMOTE`/`AFTER` for the block below figure 42, `MOVES` for single moves. A
  render-time sort used to undo them; there is none now — the order the page
  shows is the order the generator wrote.

## Fractional exponents (the experimental page)

- **The ladder runs to 30 numbers per axis** (speed degree 14, position degree
  29) and the experimental page opens there, so step ½ reaches `t^7` — fifteen
  rows instead of six. Reason: halving the step halves the top power, so double
  the rows to get back to it. Settled 2026-11-14, by the operator.
- **No grid and no inflection count off whole powers.** The page prints
  `grid n/a` and `inflections n/a`. Reason: a fractional exponent has no integer
  grid and no polynomial Wronskian, so those numbers do not exist. Settled
  2026-11-14.
- **Bend, closest and openness are measured from the curve** when the step is
  not 1.
- **Negative `t` uses the odd extension** `sign(t) |t|^(k·step)`, and the readout
  says so in words. Reason: a fractional power of a negative number is complex;
  this is a declared choice, not a silent one.
- **Mirror symmetry holds only at step 1.** Measured: mirror gap 0.0000 at step
  1, 0.42 at ½, 0.41 at ⅓, as a share of the curve's size. Reason: the speed is
  a polynomial in `t^s`, and mirroring `u` about ½ is the same as mirroring `t`
  about ½ only when `s = 1`. Do not promise balanced knots at fractional steps.
- **A fractional step cannot be symmetric at all, not merely less so.** Measured
  over 569 random rows at steps 1, ½, ¾, 3/2 and 2: not one came within 1e-3 of
  its own mirror or half turn. The reason is arithmetic, not sampling: symmetry
  needs the parameter point `t = 2^(-1/s)`, which is irrational for every
  rational step except 1. So half powers are for *new shapes*, never for
  balanced knots. Settled by measurement 2026-11-14.
- **The x row may carry its own mirrored roots.** This is the axis that adds
  loops while keeping the mirror exact: both rows are mirrored, so the curve
  stays symmetric. It produced knots with 20 meetings where the best earlier
  family reached 16, so it is the preferred way to widen the search.

## High-order tail terms loosen the knot

The low powers set the knot; a small tail at the top powers (measured on the
operator's find: `t^11` to `t^14`, coefficients of order one) opens it up and
costs the mirror.

| tail scale | crossings | knot share | mirror gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (the lace) | 13 | 4% | 0.00 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 9% | 0.28 |
| 1 (the find) | 8 | 19% | 0.51 |
| 2 | 7 | **43%** | 0.55 |
| 4 | 5 | 3% | 0.16 |
| 8 | 4 | 1% | 0.44 |

So: doubling the tail takes the knot from 19% to 43%; quadrupling it destroys the
crossings instead of loosening them. The symmetry is gone from the first step —
that is the point of the axis, and it is the only lever found so far that makes a
knot bigger without flattening the whole figure. The find is kept as
`loose-knot-tail14` in the knotlike section.

## Tweaks that keep the mirror

A row is even or odd about t = 1/2, and a tweak keeps the mirror only if it has
the same parity as the row it touches. Measured on the operator's curve: x is
even (reads the same from the far end), y is odd (reads as its own negative).

Patterns that hold the mirror, as additions at the given powers, times a size:

| row | powers | numbers |
|---|---|---|
| x (even) | t1, t2 | -1, +1 |
| x (even) | t2, t3, t4 | +1, -2, +1 |
| x (even) | t3 … t6 | +1, -3, +3, -1 |
| y (odd) | t1, t2, t3 | -1, +3, -2 |
| y (odd) | t2 … t5 | -1, +4, -5, +2 |

The operator's own habit — +0.1 on one power, −0.1 on the next — is the first
row: it works because the two changes cancel when the row is read backwards.

Multiplying a whole row by `1 + size(t − t²)` also holds the mirror, and it is the
stronger lever (crossings 13 → 19 at size 0.2). Two traps, both hit and fixed:
the product is two powers longer than the row — trimming it to the old length
drops the terms that balance the change, which is exactly the lopsided curve; and
it must be done in powers, not in boxes, because at step 1/2 a box is half a
power and the factor would centre at t = 1/4.

The experimental page carries these as buttons; the primary curve redraws at once
and `window.phNthSymmetry()` reports the mirror gap, which is 0.0000 for every
pattern above at steps 1 and 1/2.

## What a tweak costs in grid

The tweak sizes are fractions, and the fraction decides the integer grid the curve
needs. Measured on the operator's curve at step 1, adding `x: t1,t2`:

| size | grid after | factor |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 6,930 | ×2 |
| 1/4 | 22,176 | ×6.4 |
| 1/2 | 27,720 | ×8 |
| 1/8 | (cheaper than 1/4 in every case tried) | — |
| **1/3** | **86,625,000,000,000** | ruined |

1/3 is not an arithmetic limit but a machine one: a third cannot be written
exactly in binary, so every coefficient becomes a long decimal and the grid
explodes. **Only halves, quarters, eighths and whole numbers are offered**, and
the page says why. The multiply by `1 + size(t − t²)` is the most expensive
(1/2 took the grid to 5,765,760) because the factor is used twice.

The status line reports the grid after every tweak, so the cost is visible rather
than discovered later.

## A tweak is a share of the coefficient, not an absolute step

An absolute size changes every coefficient by the same amount. A share takes a
fraction of the coefficient itself, which keeps a mirrored pair balanced: the pair
has equal magnitude, so a quarter of 16 moves both ends by 4.

Measured on the default curve at step 1, adding `x: t1, t2`:

| share of the 16 pair | tweak | x becomes | grid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/16 | +1 | 3, -17, 17 | 6,930 |
| 1/8 | +2 | 3, -18, 18 | 3,465 |
| **1/4** | **+4** | 3, -20, 20 | **693** |
| 1/2 | +8 | 3, -24, 24 | 3,465 |

All keep the mirror exact. The grid is a least common multiple over the whole
position polynomial, so a share can lower it — 1/4 made the curve five times
cheaper — as well as raise it, which 1/16 did. That is the operator's gcd
instinct confirmed: the numbers have to be read together, not one at a time.

The panel offers both levers, an absolute fraction and a share of the x pair, and
the status reports the grid after every tweak.

## A rung hides numbers, it never deletes them

Moving to a lower degree keeps every coefficient above the new rung in a stash and
shows zeros in the new boxes; moving back restores them. Measured: a value of 777
in the top box at degree 29 survives degree 11 and returns on the way up. The rule
is the same everywhere in this project: a view may hide data, never destroy it.

## Half powers: a dial, not a field

Probed 2026-11-14 with `scripts/half_probe.py`; three answers, all measured.

1. **They are not a place to look for knots.** Of 400 random half-power rows, none
   had five or more crossings with a sane aspect. A half-power row is a polynomial
   in `sqrt(t)`, and its geometry collapses toward a flat band: the same numbers that
   give 38% knot at step 1 give 1% at step 1/2, with the legs at 86%.
2. **One half-power term is a useful asymmetry dial.** On a curve with six
   crossings, a value of 1 at `t^1/2` gave **nine** crossings, knot 22%, bend 2.86 —
   unbalanced (mirror gap 0.245) but knottier. At 4 it collapsed to two crossings.
   So: one or two terms in the odd boxes changes the shape deliberately; it is not
   where a search would start.
3. **The balanced tweak patterns are step-safe.** At step 1/2 they land on the
   whole-power boxes (the panel maps powers, not boxes), so the mirror stays exact:
   measured gap 0.0000 with the x pattern, the y pattern, and both, and the knot
   moves 38% → 40%, 41%, 34%. Used on an *odd* box instead they break the mirror,
   which is the dial above.
